strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and novel: constructing symmetric tree-like hierarchical features for both modalities (rather than a single visual feature vs. hierarchical textual features) and aligning them across hyperbolic manifolds with distinct learnable curvatures via an optimized intermediate manifold.

The paper provides genuine theoretical contributions: an approximate KL-based distance between heterogeneous hyperbolic manifolds, and proofs of existence and uniqueness of the optimal intermediate manifold curvature (Appendix A).

A practical optimization strategy is proposed: the golden section search for the intermediate curvature is handled via implicit function theorem gradients (Eq. 20, Algorithm 2), making the bilevel curvature optimization end-to-end trainable.

Comprehensive evaluation: four datasets, few-shot (1/16-shot) and base-to-base/base-to-novel/base-to-whole settings, three hierarchical metrics, comparisons against prompt-tuning baselines (MaPLe, PromptSRC, ProTeCt) and hyperbolic baselines (MERU, HyCoCLIP), plus ablations for each component and qualitative visualizations (t-SNE, GradCAM) that support the coarse-to-fine semantics claim.

Strong empirical gains in several settings (e.g., up to 19-28% HCA improvements in few-shot settings), and a detailed reproducibility statement with extensive implementation details and dataset construction procedures (e.g., Rare Species tree construction).
weaknesses: The theoretical results are weaker than claimed. The 'KL distance' (Theorem 1) is only an approximation obtained via a Taylor expansion around a numerically determined point (y1* ≈ 3.016), and the parameter r = ||v̄|| is asserted to be a constant despite the derivation in Eq. 26 showing it depends on c1 and c3. The existence/uniqueness proofs hold only under strong conditions on r (r > rmin, Eq. 41/44) and a lower curvature bound cmin, whose validity in practice is not verified.

The comparison in Table 2 against MERU and HyCoCLIP appears unfair. Both are hyperbolic image-text pretraining methods and were likely evaluated without prompt tuning adaptation to TOS classification, making the claimed 'up to 41% improvement' and the conclusion that hyperbolic methods have 'limited alignment ability' difficult to interpret. A properly adapted hyperbolic baseline is missing.

Ablation evidence for the central novelty (heterogeneous manifold search) is thin: in several cells the full method's advantage over Ours-HypV1/Ours-HypV2 is within ~0.1-1% (e.g., SUN 1-shot HCA 57.92 vs 57.56), and no standard deviations are reported despite averaging over three runs, so it is unclear which improvements are statistically meaningful.

There are multiple notational and typographical errors that hurt clarity: 'REALTED WORKS' in Sec. 2; the update rule for c2 in Eq. 18 is written as c2 ← c1 − η·dJ/dc1; the wrapped normal in Eq. 3 uses σ but the text defines 'u is the Frechet mean, δ > 0'; inconsistent notation for the text tree (Te vs Tc1).

The intermediate manifold objective Jc(c3) is defined on scalar global curvatures, which is a fairly restrictive notion of 'manifold distance' between distributions; the connection between this scalar-level distance and actual feature-level alignment benefit is only empirically asserted, not analyzed.

Computational overhead of the proposed modules (multi-layer token mapping, golden section search per iteration, implicit gradients) is not reported, and the sensitivity to the fixed choices of intermediate layers (4th, 7th) and loss weight α is not analyzed.

The paper claims 'consistently outperforms all baselines across all metrics and settings,' but in Table 3 several margins over ProTeCt on base/novel splits are marginal (e.g., ImageNet PromptSRC LA novel 77.15 vs 77.02, MTA novel 88.08 vs 87.90), so the claim is stronger than the evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored problem: aligning hierarchical (tree-structured) visual and textual features in VLMs, going beyond the asymmetric single-visual-feature alignment of prior work (e.g., ProTeCt).

The experimental evaluation is broad: four datasets (Cifar100, SUN, ImageNet, Rare Species), two prompt-learning backbones (MaPLe, PromptSRC), four settings (few-shot, base-to-base/novel/whole), and three standard metrics from Wu et al. (2024), with results averaged over three runs.

The attempt to define a principled distance between hyperbolic manifolds with different curvatures via KL divergence between wrapped normal distributions, plus the implicit-function-theorem gradient for the golden-section search, is a technically interesting combination.

The ablation study is structured sensibly (Euclidean / shared-curvature / per-modality-curvature variants), and visualization analyses (t-SNE, GradCAM) support the claim that intermediate-layer tokens carry coarse-to-fine semantics.
The appendix provides reasonably complete implementation details, proofs, dataset construction algorithms, and a reproducibility statement.
weaknesses: The central claim—that heterogeneous (per-modality) manifolds are the key benefit—is weakly supported by the paper's own ablations. The gain of the full method over Ours-HypV2 (shared intermediate-manifold machinery still present) is typically under 0.5% (e.g., Cifar100 16-shot LA: 77.92 vs 77.69; MTA: 90.89 vs 90.71, sometimes reversed as in Table 5 SUN 16-shot MTA 86.02 vs 85.92). Most of the improvement over ProTeCt comes from the Euclidean semantic-aware feature extraction (Ours-Euc), which is largely a combination of existing ideas (intermediate-layer tokens per Chen et al., 2024, plus text-guided cross-attention).

The theoretical contribution is more heuristic than rigorous. The 'manifold distance' (Theorem 1) relies on a first-order Taylor approximation of the arccosh distance at a numerically determined expansion point (y1* ≈ 3.016) and on r = ||v̄|| being treated as a constant although it depends on c1 and c3 (acknowledged in Eq. 26). The claimed KL-based interpretation therefore holds only approximately, and the existence/uniqueness results (Propositions 1–2) hold only under sufficient conditions on r that are never verified for the actual learned curvatures.

The visual feature 'tree' is constructed using textual hierarchical features as queries (Eq. 5), so the two trees are not independently derived; the claimed symmetry is partly circular, and the paper does not test whether the method works when hierarchical cues come from a source other than the text used for alignment.

Table 2 comparisons with MERU and HyCoCLIP are questionable: these are hyperbolic pretraining methods evaluated under very different (weaker/zero-shot or differently tuned) regimes than the proposed prompt-tuning pipeline, so margins like +25.89% LA are not meaningful evidence of superiority of the alignment mechanism.

Dataset-specific hyperparameter selection (curvature initialization from {0.5, 0.25, 0.05, 0.025}, learning rate from {0.01, 0.02, 0.03}) without sensitivity analysis raises fairness and robustness concerns; the choice of intermediate layers (4th and 7th) is also fixed without justification or ablation.

Numerous presentation errors undermine confidence: the Related Works section header is misspelled ('REALTED'), Table 1 uses 'villina' instead of 'Vanilla', Eq. (18) contains a copy-paste error ('c2 ← c1 − η·dJ/dc1'), and Theorem 1 refers to u2 although u2 is never defined (u3 is intended).

Claims of large improvements (e.g., '28.83% HCA improvement') are inflated by very low baselines (e.g., vanilla HCA of 2.97–17.54 in Table 1), and the most direct, fair comparisons (vs. ProTeCt) show much more modest and setting-dependent gains, including cases where Ours underperforms (e.g., Table 3 ImageNet base-to-novel MTA with MaPLe: 88.11 vs 88.02 is negligible; Rare Species 1-shot results are inconsistent across the two base methods).

strengths: The paper addresses a clearly motivated and underexplored problem: aligning hierarchical (tree-structured) features across both image and text modalities, rather than the asymmetric single-visual-feature vs. hierarchical-text alignment used in prior work (e.g., ProTeCt, BioCLIP).

The heterogeneous manifold alignment idea is interesting: embedding each modality in a hyperbolic manifold with its own learnable curvature and aligning them through an optimized intermediate manifold is a technically novel construction, supported by the implicit function theorem for curvature gradients.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: four datasets (CIFAR100, SUN, ImageNet, Rare Species), four settings (few-shot, base-to-base/novel/whole), three hierarchical metrics, two prompt-learning backbones (MaPLe, PromptSRC), plus comparisons against hyperbolic baselines (MERU, HyCoCLIP) and a component-wise ablation (Ours-Euc, HypV1, HypV2, full).

The ablation is well designed: Ours-Euc isolates the visual feature extraction framework, while HypV1/HypV2/full progressively isolate the effect of heterogeneous curvatures and intermediate manifold search, and results consistently support each component.

Good qualitative analysis (t-SNE at multiple taxonomic levels, GradCAM attention maps across granularities), detailed reproducibility materials (training procedures, tree construction algorithms for Rare Species and base/novel splits), and an honest LLM-usage statement.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution has gaps. The 'KL divergence between distributions on heterogeneous manifolds' is not rigorously defined—distributions live on different spaces—and Theorem 1 relies on a Taylor approximation with a numerically fixed expansion point (y* ≈ 3.016). Proposition 2's uniqueness guarantee holds only under unverified conditions on r (Eq. 44: r ≥ r*_min, etc.), and r itself is claimed constant although the midpoint norm depends on c1 and c3, creating a circularity that is not addressed. It is unclear whether these conditions hold in the actual experiments.

The reported 'affine transformation of KL divergence' is largely by definition (the distance is defined so that this holds), which weakens the claimed theoretical significance; the existence/uniqueness results are for a one-dimensional optimization and feel overstated relative to their substance.

Gains over the strongest baseline are uneven. Against ProTeCt, many cells show only marginal improvements (e.g., CIFAR100 16-shot MTA 90.89 vs. 90.79; several PromptSRC ablation cells where Ours-HypV1 or Ours-Euc underperform ProTeCt, e.g., 72.21 vs. 73.07 LA). The headline gains (up to 28.83% HCA) come largely from settings where baseline HCA is near zero, and no standard deviations or significance tests are reported despite averaging over three runs.

The comparison with MERU and HyCoCLIP (Table 2) appears potentially unfair: these are hyperbolic pretraining methods evaluated in a different regime than prompt-tuned models, and the setup for the 'ours' rows in Table 2 (which variant/backbone) is not clearly stated.

Writing and notation issues reduce clarity: 'REALTED WORKS' typo, 'villina' instead of 'vanilla' throughout Table 1, Eq. 18 contains an error (c2 ← c1 − η·dJ/dc1), inconsistent notation in the wrapped normal definition (u vs. µ, δ vs. σ), and several grammatical errors in the method section.

Hyperparameter sensitivity is underexplored: the cone constant k=0.1 is fixed without justification, curvature initialization spans an order of magnitude across datasets, and there is no analysis of sensitivity to the choice of intermediate layers (4th, 7th) or the loss weight α.

Novelty is somewhat incremental in composition: intermediate-layer ViT features (known), entailment cones (MERU/HyCoCLIP), learnable curvatures (known), and implicit differentiation (Lorraine et al.) are combined; the main novelty is the intermediate-manifold alignment formulation and its integration.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the observation that prior taxonomy-aware VLM methods align hierarchical text features with a single visual feature (asymmetric alignment), and the proposal to construct symmetric tree-like features for both modalities is a sensible and novel angle.

The heterogeneous manifold alignment is a technically interesting contribution: per-modality learnable curvatures, a KL-divergence-derived distance between hyperbolic manifolds of different curvatures, an intermediate manifold with existence/uniqueness analysis (Propositions 1-2), and a practical implicit-function-theorem gradient computation for the non-differentiable golden-section search.

Comprehensive evaluation: four datasets, four task settings (few-shot, base-to-base/novel/whole), three metrics, two prompt-learning backbones (MaPLe, PromptSRC), comparisons against ProTeCt and hyperbolic alignment methods (MERU, HyCoCLIP), and extensive ablations (cross-attention module, distance definition, layer choice, curvature initialization, r estimation, backbones, efficiency).

Substantial empirical gains, particularly on the stricter hierarchical metrics (HCA improvements up to ~28.83%), suggesting the method genuinely improves hierarchical consistency rather than only leaf accuracy.

Good supporting analyses: t-SNE and clustering metrics across taxonomic levels, GradCAM visualizations showing level-specific attention, learned curvature values across datasets, and a reproducibility statement with detailed appendices including proofs and algorithms.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is built on several approximations and heuristic choices that weaken the claimed soundness: the manifold distance relies on a first-order Taylor approximation with the expansion point y1* ≈ 3.016 chosen numerically (essentially tuned so the approximate distance has its minimizer at c3 = c1, which makes Proposition 1 somewhat circular); the constant r is defined as a function of c1 and c3 in the derivation but treated as constant; empirical relative error of the approximation reaches 32.4% in the tail (mean 5.3%). The existence/uniqueness result applies to this approximate objective over a single scalar (curvature), limiting the depth of the theory.

The intermediate manifold is parameterized by a single scalar curvature; the 'heterogeneous manifold alignment' machinery reduces to a 1D optimization solved by golden-section search. Given this simplicity, a more careful comparison or analysis against simply interpolating/averaging curvatures (the ablation compares only against (c1-c3)^2-style surrogate distances, not against a learned convex combination) would strengthen the claim that the KL-based distance is essential.

The comparison to hyperbolic alignment baselines (MERU, HyCoCLIP) is somewhat unfair/uninformative: these are not prompt-tuned for the TOS task on the same backbone, so their large gaps conflate the effect of prompt learning with the effect of the proposed alignment method.

Some gains are modest or mixed in parts of the results (e.g., small LA differences on Cifar100/PromptSRC in the generalization setting, occasional non-best values for the full method), and the paper could better characterize when the hierarchical machinery does or does not help.

The semantic-aware extraction relies on a manually chosen set of intermediate layers (4th, 7th) and disabled cross-token attention; while sensitivity analysis is provided, the design feels somewhat empirical, and the information-bottleneck justification in Appendix D is informal.

Single-curvature hyperbolic modeling limitation is acknowledged but not explored (e.g., mixed-curvature alternatives), and the method's benefit beyond taxonomy-structured labels (where trees are natural) is unclear, narrowing the scope of applicability.

strengths: The paper addresses a clearly motivated problem (asymmetric alignment between single visual features and hierarchical textual features in VLMs) and the overall framework (semantic-aware visual feature extraction + heterogeneous manifold alignment) is coherent and well-structured.

The heterogeneous manifold alignment component contains a genuine theoretical contribution: a KL-based distance between hyperbolic manifolds with distinct curvatures, a proof of the soundness of this distance (Proposition 1), and existence/uniqueness of the optimal intermediate manifold (Proposition 2), with efficient curvature gradient computation via the implicit function theorem.

The experimental evaluation is extensive: four datasets, four evaluation settings (few-shot, base-to-base, base-to-novel, base-to-whole), three metrics, two prompt-learning backbones (MaPLe, PromptSRC), comparisons against both Euclidean (ProTeCt) and hyperbolic (MERU, HyCoCLIP) baselines, plus thorough ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity analyses, efficiency analysis, and qualitative visualizations (t-SNE, GradCAM).

The appendices are unusually thorough, including approximation-error analysis of the Taylor expansion, analysis of the constant r, an alternative Rare Species labeling strategy, class-imbalance analysis, and detailed reproducibility material.
weaknesses: The theoretical results are fragile: Theorem 1 relies on a first-order Taylor approximation with an expansion point chosen numerically (y* ≈ 3.016), treats r as a constant even though it depends on c1 and c3, and the propositions hold only under additional conditions on r (Eq. 41, 44). The empirical approximation error reaches up to 32%, so the 'existence and uniqueness' guarantees apply to an approximation rather than the actual distance, which weakens the claimed mathematical contribution.

Gains over the strongest baseline (ProTeCt) are often small and inconsistent in magnitude: LA improvements are frequently below 1 point (e.g., 85.36→85.58 on Cifar100 base-to-novel; 78.76→78.90 on 16-shot Cifar100), some metrics slightly regress (Cifar100 PromptSRC HCA novel 40.02 vs 40.12; several MTA novel entries), and no standard deviations or statistical significance tests are reported despite averaging over three runs, making many claims of 'consistently outperforms' hard to verify.

The ablation of the core novelty is not fully convincing: the gap between Ours-HypV2 (independent per-modality curvatures) and the full method (intermediate manifold search) is typically only ~0.1–0.7 points, raising questions about whether the theoretically elaborate intermediate-manifold machinery is worth its added complexity.

The central claim that asymmetric alignment causes suboptimal alignment is supported only by an illustrative figure and citations, not by direct evidence or analysis quantifying the asymmetry problem.

Scope and novelty are somewhat limited: both main ingredients build on well-established ideas (intermediate ViT layers encode coarse semantics; hyperbolic entailment cones from MERU/HyCoCLIP), evaluation is confined to prompt-tuning on CLIP within a single task family (TOS classification largely from Wu et al., 2024), and one evaluation setting (base-to-novel tree partitioning) is proposed by the authors themselves, limiting external comparability.

The manifold distance derivation defines a 'distance' that is not a metric (asymmetric, violates triangle inequality), and the paper's motivation for needing a principled inter-manifold distance is undercut by the fact that simple baselines like squared log distance perform nearly as well (Table 8).

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and well-motivated problem: existing prompt-learning methods for taxonomic open-set (TOS) classification use asymmetric alignment (hierarchical text features vs. a single visual feature). Proposing symmetric tree-to-tree alignment on hyperbolic manifolds is a sensible and interesting direction.

The heterogeneous manifold alignment formulation is technically thoughtful: per-modality learnable curvatures, a KL-based manifold distance over wrapped normal distributions, an intermediate manifold with proven existence/uniqueness of the optimal curvature, and implicit-function-theorem gradients through the golden-section search form a coherent optimization pipeline (Algorithm 2).

The empirical evaluation is extensive and convincing: four datasets, 1-shot/16-shot, base-to-base/novel/whole generalization, three hierarchical metrics, two prompt-learning backbones (MaPLe, PromptSRC), and a deeper backbone (ViT-L/14). Gains over the strong ProTeCt baseline are consistent, e.g., up to +19% LA and +28.83% HCA in the 16-shot setting, and large improvements over hyperbolic alignment baselines (MERU, HyCoCLIP).

The ablation study is well designed and thorough: Euclidean vs. shared-curvature vs. per-modality-curvature vs. full method (Tables 3, 6, 7), ablation of the manifold distance definition (Table 8), cross-attention module (Table 9), intermediate layer choice, curvature initialization, loss weight, and the approximation constant r (Tables 11, 12, 14), plus efficiency analysis showing negligible overhead.

Additional analyses strengthen credibility: quantified Taylor-approximation error (~5.3% mean relative error over 1M pairs), per-batch estimation of r, learned curvature values per dataset (Table 18) supporting the core motivation, quantitative clustering metrics for learned hierarchical representations, alternative Rare Species labeling strategy, and class-imbalance analysis.
Good reproducibility posture: detailed experimental settings, algorithms for tree construction and training, and a stated commitment to open-source code and models.
weaknesses: The theoretical contributions are weaker than claimed. 'Theorem 1' is not an exact result but a Taylor-approximated expression with a numerically solved expansion point (y*≈3.016) and an assumed constant r; Propositions 1 and 2 hold only under sufficient conditions on r (e.g., r >= rmin, Eq. 41/44) whose satisfaction in practice is not verified. The claim of 'existence and uniqueness of the optimal intermediate manifold' in the abstract overstates the rigor of the underlying result.

The definition of the manifold distance has internal inconsistencies: the final closed form D_L depends only on curvatures, but this requires assuming r = ||v̄|| is constant even though the authors note it depends on c1 and c3, and it assumes the Frechet means u1, u3 are aligned in a specific way (mapped via the exponential map at the origin). The conditions under which Eq. (9) remains an affine transformation of the KL divergence are heuristic.

The marginal contribution of the intermediate manifold over the simpler per-modality curvature variant is small in ablations (e.g., 16-shot MaPLe Cifar100: Ours-HypV2 77.69/69.33 vs. Ours 77.92/69.38; SUN 75.19/68.65 vs. 75.47/68.67; Rare Species even slightly lower on HCA). Since the intermediate manifold is the paper's most novel algorithmic component, its added value appears limited, and the difference between HypV2 and Ours is within likely run-to-run variance (no statistical significance tests are reported).

The method is largely an incremental combination of existing techniques: intermediate-layer features from ViT, cross-attention guided by text queries, entailment cones from MERU/HyCoCLIP, and the ProTeCt contrastive objective. The semantic-aware extraction module (disabling cross-token self-attention after layer p_j) is interesting but the information-bottleneck justification in Appendix D.1 is loose and would not survive on its own.

Some evaluation details raise questions: the base-to-novel setting is newly proposed by the authors with tuned hyperparameters (10 epochs 'to maintain generalizability'), and on Cifar100 with PromptSRC the gains on LA/MTA are marginal (85.58 vs. 85.36; 85.37 vs. 84.88 HM), so broad generalization claims rest mostly on HCA improvements. Also, 'up to X%' improvements appear cherry-picked from the best dataset/setting cell (Rare Species 16-shot).

Clarity issues in the main text: the derivation pipeline (Eq. 22–32) is spread across the appendix with the main-body theorem stated without indication that it is an approximation; the loss notation reuses J_ent for different pairings; and Eq. (13)'s exterior-angle expression is hard to verify at a glance. The paper would benefit from a more precise framing of what is exact versus approximate.

No code is provided at review time despite the commitment, and comparison with the very recent geometry-aware hierarchical alignment work (Li et al., 2025a, cited) is only briefly discussed rather than empirically compared.
